lessonTitle: Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions and separation of duty
md: Giving a reporting job or an engineer direct write access to production tables quietly turns them into an uncertified TP. Read-only replicas for reporting, and audited break-glass access for emergencies, keep rule E1 true.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Case: VPN appliances under attack, Pulse 2021 and Ivanti 2024
md: Mitigation is not remediation. Volexity's disclosure warned that a mitigation "does not remedy a past or ongoing compromise". After an edge device is exploited, assume its secrets and its users' credentials are gone, and rotate them.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Compression has costs of its own. The compressor runs on the critical path of every request. The compressed text is hard for humans to read, which makes debugging and audits harder. Exact strings (code, JSON, numbers, IDs) can be damaged by token deletion. And question-aware compression produces a different context for every question, so that context can no longer be served from the provider's prefix cache.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell: how logging a string ran code
md: Only `log4j-core` 2.x is affected; applications with just `log4j-api` are not, and Log4j 1.x has no lookups (its separate JMSAppender issue is CVE-2021-4104). But Log4j is often a *transitive* dependency: a library you use pulls it in, so "we do not use Log4j" needs checking, not assuming.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (a general-purpose malloc used by FreeBSD and Firefox, among others) and in glibc malloc (the GNU C library's allocator, the default on most Linux systems) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
md: The colocated code keeps a comment worth remembering: SGLang returns from the update request after enqueueing GPU copies, not after they finish. Reusing the same flattened IPC buffer for the next bucket right away could overwrite memory SGLang is still reading and corrupt weights, so slime allocates a fresh buffer per bucket.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
md: Enrichment answers "what is this thing?", not "is this bad?". Treat every enriched field as a claim with a source and an age, show unknowns explicitly, and never let a single reputation score close or escalate an alert by itself.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
md: Never let an attacker-controlled message decide who you trust. A chat message saying "I'm from IT, please approve the prompt" is exactly what the Lapsus$ actors sent, per the CSRB. The same rule applies inside the SOC: verify urgent requests to disable monitoring or grant access through a second channel.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
md: Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$, where norm rescales to sum to 1. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: Read a pointer as five numbers: four 9-bit table indices and a 12-bit offset. Huge pages simply end the walk early and widen the offset to 21 or 30 bits.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
md: Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature and top-k.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: pipefail meets SIGPIPE: with pipefail on, `yes | head -n 1` has status 141, because yes was killed when head exited. `seq 1 3 | head -n 1` returns 0 only because all its output fit in the pipe before head quit. Under `set -e`, a producer piped into `head` can end the script on large inputs; test such pipelines at realistic sizes.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: More cores does not mean every program runs faster. If each operation reads a lot of data and does little math per byte, the SMs wait on HBM no matter how many there are. The next lesson turns this into a number.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values (the CPU's working slots, lesson 2), and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Ranking with vectors and cosine similarity
md: The vector space model scores a document by the cosine between its tf-idf vector and the query's. Engines compute it by streaming the query terms' postings into accumulators, so documents that share no query term cost nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: A hidden layer only adds power because of the nonlinearity between layers. Without it, any stack of layers is one linear map in disguise.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
md: The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window (the most tokens the model can read and write in one pass) caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs
md: Learned memory turns the state of a recurrent layer into a model trained online. You choose its architecture, objective, forgetting and optimizer; you pay for expressiveness in wall-clock time, and you still pair it with attention for exact local recall.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack surface: every door, window and vent
md: "Internal only" is not off the surface. An endpoint reachable only from inside the network is still reachable by anyone who gets inside: a phished employee, a compromised vendor login, a malicious insider. Count it, and protect it as if the network were hostile.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Third-party access is a trust boundary you do not fully control. Give each vendor the narrowest path, watch it closely, and assume the vendor's own computers may already be compromised.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A forecast is a prediction made at an origin $T$ using only data up to $T$, for a stated horizon $h$. Every evaluation in this course respects that constraint.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
md: Common misconception: "the CN must match the hostname". Modern clients ignore CN for name matching and check SAN only; a certificate with the right CN but no matching SAN entry fails in browsers and in Python's ssl module.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Your first kernel: program_id, offsets and masks
md: `tl.load` with a mask but no `other=` leaves masked lanes **undefined**. That is safe only if those lanes never feed a result. Any reduction (sum, max) over a masked block needs `other=` set to the operation's neutral value: the value that leaves the result unchanged, 0 for a sum (x + 0 = x) and minus infinity for a max (max(x, -inf) = x).

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
md: Misconception: "lambda is just a weight, any value works." Text cross-entropy and noise MSE live on different scales, and lambda decides how the shared weights split their capacity. Transfusion used 5, BAGEL effectively 4 (0.25 CE + 1 MSE is a quarter of CE + 4 MSE). Change the noise parameterization or schedule and the right value moves.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
md: Build-time specialization = **pick components by configuration, link statically, let DCE and LTO remove the rest**. Reconfiguring means rebuilding.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: Remember the condition that makes resharding free: choose generation groups so that **each GPU's generation shard contains its training shard**. Then the only traffic is one all-gather per micro DP group, and no GPU keeps a second copy.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: The dynamics model: next-frame tokens with MaskGIT
md: Generating a frame is not one forward pass. Each frame costs a full MaskGIT loop (25 passes in Genie) over a context that grows with every frame. The paper's own limitations: Genie runs at around 1 FPS and is limited to 16 frames of memory.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads
md: CORS is enforced by **browsers**, about **reading**. It is not access control on your server. `curl` or a script outside a browser ignores it completely, and a simple request reaches your server even when the browser will later hide the response. Authentication and authorization still have to happen on the server for every request.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity
md: SIDs, not names, are what Windows checks. A renamed Administrator still has RID 500, and a deleted and re-created account gets a new SID, so it does not inherit the old account's permissions.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake
md: Messages 1 and 2 move the nonces; messages 3 and 4 deliver the group key and confirm the keys, which is also how the handshake protects against downgrades. The PMK itself never crosses the air, but everything else that goes into the PTK does.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package
md: Obfuscating a hardcoded secret (splitting it, XORing it, hiding it in native code) only slows an analyst down; the app must reconstruct it to use it, so an attacker with the app can too. If a value must stay secret from users, it must not be in the app.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
md: The searching count throttles wakeups, and the barrier on both sides of it prevents lost ones. Remove the throttle and you get a thundering herd; remove the barrier and you get stranded tasks with idle cores.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
md: Pipes are the kernel's zero-copy buffer: slots of reference-counted page pointers. splice moves those pointers between a pipe and any descriptor, tee duplicates them, and sendfile itself runs on this machinery with a hidden internal pipe.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Constrain the LLM to the label set, read a probability per label, and divide by the probabilities a content-free input gets under the same prompt. Calibration fixes a constant shift; it cannot fix a model that does not understand the labels.
